wines.name: Rosé

window.note: 2012 was a small, superb Champagne vintage. A vintage rosé at fourteen years is at its savoury apex — gorgeous now, and it will cruise past 2030 if kept cool and dark.

rating.basis: estimated — matches the verified critic consensus of 91–94 for the 2012

wines.notes: Mature vintage rosé in full voice: the salmon pink is edging toward onion skin, wild strawberry and blood orange have picked up brioche, hazelnut and a savoury pinot depth, and the mousse has softened to cream. Assembled the old way — half Pinot Noir, a third Chardonnay, and a dose of still Bouzy red for colour. More a wine with bubbles than a party sparkler — serve it not too cold.
wines.pairing_classic: Potée champenoise — the harvest-day pot of ham, sausage and cabbage the pickers eat — or simply a roast chicken with tarragon.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Lechon, skin priority — cochinillo if you're in Spain. The mousse scrubs the fat, the pinot core stands up to the roast, and a fourteen-year-old rosé has enough savoury depth to talk to the liver sauce.

anecdotes.text: Pol Roger was Winston Churchill's champagne — he bought it by the pallet, named a racehorse after it (the horse won), and called the house's address 'the world's most drinkable'. When he died in 1965, Pol Roger put a black border on every label shipped to Britain, and later named its prestige cuvée Sir Winston Churchill.

The royal warrant on the shoulder — 'By Appointment to H.M. Queen Elizabeth II' — wasn't ceremonial: Pol Roger poured at the 2011 wedding of William and Kate. The house kept the late Queen's warrant on bottlings from her era.

In February 1900 Pol Roger's Épernay cellars caved in overnight, swallowing about 1.5 million bottles and five hundred casks. The house dug new cellars 33 metres down — among the deepest and coldest in Champagne, part of why its wines age so slowly.

2012 nearly didn't happen: frost, hail and mildew wrecked the spring, then a flawless late summer saved a tiny, concentrated crop. Growers rank it with 2002 and 2008 among the century's best — small harvest, long memory.

wines.name: Bordeaux

window.note: Branded AOC Bordeaux runs five to eight years; 2018's ripeness bought it the extra year, and that year is now up.

wines.notes: Merlot-led claret in its easy chair: plum, cedar shavings, a little tobacco leaf, tannins already melted. It hit its stride around 2023 and is coasting now — open it, don't cellar it, and keep the decant short.
wines.pairing_classic: Entrecôte à la bordelaise — ribeye under the red-wine shallot sauce, the city's own bistro standard.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Tortang talong with giniling. Smoky grilled eggplant does for mellow Merlot what char always does — it adds back the savoury edge the wine has traded for softness.

anecdotes.text: The dragon-prowed boat is Château Beychevelle's emblem. Legend has it ships on the Gironde lowered their sails — baisse-voile — to salute the estate's owner, the Duke of Épernon, Grand Admiral of France; the château's name and the boat both come from that salute. Grand Bateau is the Beychevelle team's everyday label.

2018 in Bordeaux was a rescue story: a mildew-soaked spring that ruined nerves and some crops, then a scorching summer that saved everything left. Growers say they aged a decade in six months and then made one of the ripest vintages of the era.

wines.name: Soul of the Andes Reserva Carménère

window.note: Entry-level reserva built for early drinking; the herbal edge gets louder rather than softer with age.

wines.notes: Deep purple and unmistakably Carménère: blackberry and plum over roasted red pepper, sweet paprika and a dusting of cocoa. Soft-grained tannin, made to be friendly young — not a wine to overthink, a wine to pour.
wines.pairing_classic: Chilean asado with pebre, or empanadas de pino — beef, olive, raisin and boiled egg, the national handful.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Crispy duck in hoisin wraps. The grape's roasted-pepper note behaves like an extra spoonful of hoisin, and the wine's plushness rides the pancake's sweetness.

anecdotes.text: Carménère is Bordeaux's lost grape. Phylloxera wiped it from France in the 1860s and it was presumed extinct — until 1994, when ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot looked at a Chilean 'Merlot' vineyard and realized half of it was Carménère that had been hiding under the wrong name for a century.
Carménère comes from carmin — crimson — for the scarlet blaze of its leaves each autumn. Vineyards of it look like they're on fire in May, Chile's autumn.
Ventisquero means 'glacier' — the winery named itself after the ice fields of the southern Andes, and its top wines all carry mountain imagery. The climber on this label is the house's signature.

wines.name: Reserva Cabernet Sauvignon

window.note: Reserva-level Chilean cabernet is best inside five or six years, while the fruit still leads the herbs.

rating.basis: estimated — tempered by a weak Vivino community showing

sources.detail: 2021 vintage attribution; ratings count not visible

wines.notes: Cassis and dried herbs with a graphite line down the middle; medium-bodied, brisk acidity off cool Andean nights, a clean and faintly dusty finish. Honest Tuesday cabernet that punches at its price.
wines.pairing_classic: Plateada al horno — Chile's slow-roasted brisket cap, collapsing into its own juices.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Filipino barbecue skewers with the banana-ketchup glaze charred at the edges — the sweet-sour lacquer locks onto the cassis and the grill smoke ties the knot.

anecdotes.text: Sanama is a label of Château Los Boldos, a French-founded Cachapoal Andes estate (formerly Viña Santa Amalia) owned since 2008 by Portugal's Sogrape — the family firm behind Mateus and Sandeman. A Chilean wine with a French name and a Portuguese parent.

Cachapoal Andes is the foothill side of the valley, where cold mountain air pours down every night — the swing between afternoon and dawn can pass 20°C. That free refrigeration is why Chilean cabernet at this price still tastes fresh.

'Reserva' on a Chilean label is a courtesy, not a law — unlike Spain, where the word is policed with minimum barrel and bottle time. In Chile it mostly means 'the step above our base wine'. Useful to know before it impresses anyone.

Chile is one of the last places on earth where Cabernet grows on its own roots. Phylloxera never made it past the Atacama, the Andes and the Pacific, so vines here skip the grafting every European vineyard depends on.

wines.name: Rüdesheimer Berg Rottland Spätburgunder GG

window.note: Grosses Gewächs Spätburgunder from the warm 2018 vintage: open now, with the tertiary spice due after 2027.

rating.basis: estimated — the one vintage-specific guide score runs a notch cooler

sources.detail: 2018 vintage — the only vintage-specific score found; beware conflation with the higher-scored Berg Schlossberg GG

wines.notes: German Pinot at full stretch: black cherry and rosehip, forest floor, a smoky mineral thread off the slate-and-quartzite slope above Rüdesheim. Silkier than village Burgundy at the same age, with 2018's warmth filling out the mid-palate.
wines.pairing_classic: The St. Martin's Day goose with Rotkohl — or Rheinischer Sauerbraten, the Rhine's sweet-sour pot roast.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Unagi kabayaki over rice. The eel's sweet soy glaze and charcoal edge are exactly what silky Spätburgunder wants — a sommelier party trick that never misses.

anecdotes.text: This may be the world's oldest working wine estate: Cistercian monks founded Kloster Eberbach in 1136 and it has brought in a harvest every year since — nearly nine hundred vintages. Today it's run as the Hessian state winery.

The German wine term Kabinett was born in this cellar. From 1730 the abbey locked its finest casks in a vault called the Cabinet — the Cabinetkeller on this label — and 'Cabinet wine' eventually became a legal category for the whole country.

The Name of the Rose was filmed in the abbey — the monastery interiors around Sean Connery are Kloster Eberbach's real cloisters and dormitory. The winery leans into it; there's a wine named Umberto in the shop.
Berg Rottland takes its name from roden — 'to clear'. It's the medieval clearing above Rüdesheim, vines since at least the 11th century, and one of the warmest slopes on the Rhine.

wines.name: Brave New World Shiraz Black

window.note: Dense regional McLaren Vale shiraz holds on fruit through the late 2020s; no reward for waiting past that.

rating.basis: estimated — in line with community data

wines.notes: McLaren Vale in one glass: blackberry jam cut with dark chocolate, licorice and a eucalyptus lift. 'Black' is truth in labelling — inky, plush, generously oaked, zero minimalism.
wines.pairing_classic: Barbecued lamb chops with charred rosemary — or kangaroo fillet, if you're being properly South Australian.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Char siu, burnt ends included. Maltose lacquer and five-spice meet shiraz jam and sweet oak — the same flavour built from two directions.

anecdotes.text: The 'brave new world' is Thomas Hardy's own story: he landed in Adelaide in 1850, twenty years old, drove cattle for wages, and by 1853 owned river land at Bankside. He died the acknowledged father of the South Australian wine industry.

McLaren Vale shiraz genuinely tastes of dark chocolate — it's the region's calling card, from warm ripening over ancient soils. Locals lean into it and serve the wines with chocolate desserts, which sounds wrong and works.
This line lives almost entirely in travel retail — it's a wine that has passed through more duty-frees than most pilots. If it looks unfamiliar in shops, that's why.

wines.name: Los Prados

window.note: 2015 was a warm, excellent Rioja vintage; a reserva-level Alavesa tempranillo sits on its plateau for most of a decade.

rating.basis: estimated — direct 2015 scores are scarce; the sibling 2016 medalled

wines.notes: Modern Rioja Alavesa: black cherry with balsamic depth, vanilla and a coconut whisper from oak that has now folded in, chalk-fine tannin off limestone under the Sierra de Cantabria. Eleven years on it's fully assembled.
wines.pairing_classic: Chuletillas al sarmiento — milk-fed lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings — or patatas a la riojana when it's cold.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Beef kaldereta. The liver-spread richness in the sauce is practically Rioja's soulmate — tempranillo's acid cuts it, the oak's vanilla rounds the chilli.

anecdotes.text: Ysios is as famous for architecture as wine: Santiago Calatrava built the bodega in 2001 as a 200-metre wave of cedar and aluminium that mirrors the Sierra de Cantabria ridge behind it. People drive to Laguardia just to photograph the roof.

That beautiful roof leaked. Badly enough that in 2013 the winery sued Calatrava over a repair bill reported around two million euros — a good line to have ready as the wine breathes: the wave was better to look at than to stand under.
Ysios fuses Isis and Osiris, the Egyptian gods of rebirth — the house's founding conceit as a millennium project. Los Prados, 'the meadows', names the home parcels around the winery.

wines.name: 1853 Special Bin 858 Shiraz

window.note: Multi-region South Australian shiraz at this tier is best inside seven or eight years; it's in the last stretch of peak now.

rating.basis: estimated — anchored to Wine Enthusiast's 90 for this exact vintage

wines.notes: A broader South Australian blend than its McLaren Vale sibling — 51% Barossa, 48% Clare Valley, a splash of McLaren Vale: black plum, mocha and sweet baking spice, rounder and softer through the middle. Built to please tonight rather than to reward patience.
wines.pairing_classic: A proper Aussie barbecue: beef short ribs, burnt snags, no apologies.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Beef tapa, garlic rice, spiced vinegar — breakfast-for-dinner. The vinegar snap resets the wine's fruit-sweetness with every bite.

anecdotes.text: 'Bin' is Australian cellar bookkeeping: numbered storage bays where batches waited in bottle. Naming wines for their bin number — Penfolds Bin 28, this Bin 858 — started as warehouse admin and calcified into marketing tradition.

You hold two Hardys 2019 shiraz: this blend (51% Barossa, 48% Clare, 1% McLaren Vale) and the all-McLaren Vale 'Black'. Pour them blind side by side and taste exactly what one region adds — it's a ready-made party game.

2019 was the first vintage of the 1853 line — an Asia-market exclusive that never sees a European shelf. Wine Enthusiast gave this debut 90 points, which for a duty-free-corridor wine is quietly impressive.

wines.name: Pinot Noir

window.note: Everyday NZ pinot trades on freshness — earlier is simply better. Drink over the coming year.

rating.basis: estimated — in line with community data

sources.detail: ~290 ratings, Hawke's Bay cuvée page, all vintages

wines.notes: Light, bright, red-fruited: cherry cola, cranberry, a leafy edge. Simple in the good sense of the word — serve it cool and it does its job without ceremony.
wines.pairing_classic: Lamb rump with kūmara mash — Hawke's Bay is lamb country before it is wine country.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Slightly chilled, next to inihaw na liempo straight off the grill with a calamansi-soy dip. Light pinot loves char far more than people expect.

anecdotes.text: Hawke's Bay is Syrah and Bordeaux-blend country — New Zealand's pinot fame lives south, in Martinborough and Central Otago. A Hawke's Bay pinot is the region playing an away game, which is a more interesting fact than most budget labels carry.

This is New Zealand's oldest wine region: French Marist missionaries planted at Mission Estate in 1851, and the winery they founded still operates — it was pouring wine before the country had railways.

In 1867 a flood shifted the Ngaruroro River overnight and left behind 800 hectares of bony riverbed nobody wanted. That reject land — the Gimblett Gravels — is now the most valuable vineyard dirt in New Zealand.

wines.name: Filsell Shiraz

window.note: Old-vine Barossa shiraz from a measured, drought-concentrated vintage; a decade is comfortable, now through 2029 is the sweet spot.

rating.basis: estimated — centred in a verified 88–95 critic spread for this vintage

wines.notes: Old-vine Barossa density without the syrup: blackberry and dark plum, licorice, cedar, tannin with the grain of turned leather. The concentration comes from vine age rather than winemaking force, and you can taste the difference.
wines.pairing_classic: Shiraz-braised beef cheeks with a side of mettwurst — the Barossa's Silesian settlers still smoke their own.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Bulgogi in lettuce cups with ssamjang. Sweet soy beef and plush old-vine shiraz shake hands, and the ssamjang's funk gives the finish somewhere to go.

anecdotes.text: The Filsell vineyard's shiraz was planted around the 1920s — dry-grown, ungrafted vines now past their century. Barossa holds some of the oldest producing shiraz on earth because phylloxera never reached South Australia.
Filsell fruit is the backbone of Meshach, Grant Burge's flagship. Same vineyard, fraction of the price — this bottle is the flagship's engine room with less oak and less waiting.

Grant Burge is fifth-generation Barossa; the first Burge arrived in the valley in the 1850s. The label's 'honouring the 1865 pioneer' points at Meshach Burge, the great-grandfather the flagship is named for.

wines.name: Sauternes

window.note: Well-made Sauternes from a fine vintage; already golden and generous, with a decade of upside left. No hurry whatsoever.

rating.basis: estimated — centred in the verified 90–93 critic band for the 2015

wines.notes: Apricot, saffron and candied orange peel carried on the honeyed weight of real botrytis. 2015 supplied richness; the acid keeps it from cloying. The colour is deepening toward amber, right on schedule.
wines.pairing_classic: Foie gras mi-cuit — the Sud-Ouest's own handshake — or Roquefort to close the meal.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Leche flan with a few flakes of sea salt on top. Same caramel register as the wine — and the salt is the trick, it makes the botrytis taste twice as complex.

anecdotes.text: Sauternes exists because of a stream: the cold, spring-fed Ciron meets the warmer Garonne every autumn morning and blankets the vines in mist. The fog feeds noble rot, the afternoon sun concentrates it, and each shrivelled vine yields roughly one glass of wine.

Pickers walk the same rows again and again — five or six passes, selecting berry by berry, taking only fruit the fungus has properly raisined. It's the closest thing in wine to harvesting with tweezers, which is why honest Sauternes is never cheap to make.

Bastor-Lamontagne's paper trail reaches back to 1711, when the land answered to the French crown. It has never held classed-growth rank, which is exactly why it's the insider's Sauternes — the quality climbed while the price stayed on the ground.

wines.name: Unterstenberg Riesling № 12

window.note: Grosse Lage Saar riesling with the acid spine for fifteen years; it has just entered its best decade.

rating.basis: estimated — bracketed by Mosel Fine Wines' 91 and a merchant 92+

sources.detail: 2022 — merchant score, not a major critic

wines.notes: Saar riesling on a knife's edge: white peach and lime pith over crushed slate, a breath of sweetness that reads as texture rather than sugar, and a long saline tail. Twelve percent alcohol and it feels weightless.
wines.pairing_classic: Forelle Müllerin — pan-fried river trout with brown butter and almonds, the Saar's own fish.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Sinuglaw — grilled pork belly folded into fish kinilaw. Smoke, vinegar sour, a little chilli: the gently off-dry Saar style might as well have been designed for it.

anecdotes.text: Lauer names its wines after casks. Every cuvée carries the number of the barrel — Fass — it historically filled, and № 12 has meant the Unterstenberg parcel for generations. Cellar bookkeeping became the house's entire identity.
Unterstenberg is a parcel of the great Ayler Kupp slope, much of it on old ungrafted vines — plantings from before grafting became standard, still on their own roots in the Saar's cold slate.

The Saar was German wine's cold edge — a generation ago it fully ripened maybe three years in ten, and those rare successes became legends. Climate change quietly turned the region from gamble to sweet spot, and prices haven't fully noticed yet.

wines.name: Ayl Riesling № 21

window.note: Dry Erste Lage riesling: excellent on release, gains savoury depth toward the end of the decade.

rating.basis: estimated — coverage is thin because this is the debut bottling

sources.detail: 2022 — merchant score, not a major critic; the only number found

wines.notes: Bone-dry and quietly stern: green apple, fennel, wet stone, a chalk-dust grip on the finish. The circled T on the fine print means trocken — this is the house's serious dry table wine, built for food more than the terrace. 2022 was this bottling's debut: Lauer's first-ever dry Erste Lage, which is why the critics hadn't caught up to it yet.
wines.pairing_classic: A Winzervesper — smoked ham, young cheese, dark bread: the growers' lunch this style was built for.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Chicken inasal with blistered skin and the chili-calamansi dip. Bone-dry riesling is the condiment that table has always been missing.

anecdotes.text: Your two Lauers teach the whole German classification: this one is Erste Lage — premier cru, from the Scheidterberg above Ayl — and № 12 is Grosse Lage, grand cru. The VDP borrowed Burgundy's ladder rung for rung; pour both and the hierarchy explains itself.

Dry Saar riesling barely existed a generation ago — the region rarely got grapes ripe enough to ferment fully dry without the wine turning sour. A confident trocken from Ayl is a small climate-history document in a glass.

wines.name: Steinberger Goldener Becher Riesling GG

window.note: Young grand cru riesling from a monopole site: approachable now, but the real material arrives from 2027 and holds for a decade beyond.

rating.basis: estimated — the 2022 itself is unrated; neighbouring vintages run 92–97

sources.detail: 2021 debut vintage, NOT this 2022 — the producer reuses the quote

wines.notes: From the heart of the walled Steinberg: yellow orchard fruit, lemon oil, a smoky wet-stone line, dry and vertical. Monumental mostly in outline right now — the detail fills in from 2027 and it will outlive most of the reds in this cellar.
wines.pairing_classic: Zander in riesling cream sauce — Rhine fish poached in Rhine wine, the Rheingau's own logic.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Hainanese chicken rice with the ginger-scallion sauce. Great dry riesling speaks ginger as a first language.

anecdotes.text: The Steinberg is Germany's Clos Vougeot: monks spent roughly two centuries raising a three-kilometre stone wall around one vineyard, finishing in the 1760s. It has been a monopole — one owner, one wine — for nearly nine hundred years. MONOPOL on the label is the entire flex.

Goldener Becher — 'the golden cup' — is the prime heart of the enclosure, the parcel the estate bottles as its grand cru. Vineyard names inside a walled monopole are like room names inside a family house: only insiders use them, which is what makes dropping one fun.

The monks who built this came from Burgundy in 1136, sent by Bernard of Clairvaux's order, and brought their vine-growing doctrine with them. Rheingau riesling and grand cru Burgundy are cousins raised by the same religious order.

If anyone quotes '97 points' at this bottle, check the fine print: Stuart Pigott's famous 97 went to the 2021 debut vintage, and the estate happily reprints the quote beside every later release. Your 2022 is, as of mid-2026, unrated by any major critic — a blank spot on a famous wine.

wines.name: Ayler Riesling № 2

window.note: Dry village-tier Saar riesling: brilliant young, holds to decade's end. Drunk at eighteen months — early prime.

rating.basis: estimated — no confirmed score exists for the 2022

sources.detail: listed on the producer's page without a vintage — likely a later release, not confirmed for 2022

wines.notes: The house's dry village wine: green apple, white herbs and slate, Lauer's signature tension at twelve percent, finished with the ⓣ of a proper trocken. Fass 2 is the straightforward one in the range — as straightforward as the Saar ever gets.
wines.pairing_classic: Dibbelabbes — the Saarland's potato, leek and dried-beef hash, scraped crisp from the pan.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Sinigang na hipon. Tamarind sourness against dry riesling acidity is a handshake between equals — neither blinks, both win.

anecdotes.text: This was the collection's fourth Peter Lauer: № 2 and Senior № 6 drunk (village tier, dry and off-dry), № 21 Erste Lage and № 12 Grosse Lage still racked. One grower from one Saar village, four casks deep — the habit is official.

№ 2 and Senior № 6 are the same village, grape, tier and vintage, split only by style — this one trocken, the Senior gently sweet in the grandfather's taste. Drinking them eighteen months apart was a controlled experiment run by accident.

The a.p.nr. on the label — 3501074/02/23 — is Germany's official lot number: the /23 says this exact bottling passed the state tasting panel in 2023. German wine carries its own paperwork trail, printed in plain sight.

wines.name: Ariyanas Seco sobre Lías Finas

window.note: Aromatic dry white on lees: best in its first four years. Drunk at three — well timed.

rating.basis: estimated — inside the cuvée's cross-vintage record of 88–92

wines.notes: Dry Muscat is a high-wire act, and this one walked it: all the orange-blossom, lychee and grape-skin perfume of Moscatel with none of the sugar, the fine lees adding a waxy, saline middle. From slate terraces above Málaga so steep the work is still done by mule.
wines.pairing_classic: Espetos — sardines grilled on cane skewers, the Málaga beach ritual.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Kinilaw with green mango. The wine's perfume mirrors the fruit while staying bone dry, and the vinegar sharpens both.

anecdotes.text: Bentomiz is a Dutch love story: Clara Verheij and André Both found abandoned slate terraces in the Axarquía hills in the 1990s and rebuilt a wine region bottle by bottle. Their cellar door serves some of the best food in rural Málaga.

Moscatel de Alejandría may be the oldest cultivated wine grape still in commercial production — Phoenician traders moved it through Málaga's port millennia ago. Málaga's fame was built on the sweet version; making it bone-dry is the modern rebellion.

Málaga was the first wine region in Spain that phylloxera destroyed — the louse landed there in 1878 and erased a world-famous industry within a decade. Every modern Axarquía bottle is a revival act on century-abandoned terraces.

Per the producer, Ariyanas has featured on the tasting menu at El Celler de Can Roca — twice named the world's best restaurant — since 2011. You drank the wine the Roca brothers pour with their tasting menu, at home, with takeout-level ceremony. Correct.

wines.name: Senior Ayler Riesling № 6

window.note: Ortswein-tier Saar riesling: charming young, comfortably good to 2030. Drunk in its prime.

rating.basis: estimated — lands exactly on Mosel Fine Wines' 89

wines.notes: Lauer's crowd-pleaser with the house signature intact: yellow apple and herbs on slatey drive, 11% alcohol, a kiss of sweetness tuned to read nearly dry. Village tier — but the village is Ayl, so it drinks above its rank.
wines.pairing_classic: Schweinebraten with bread dumplings — the German Sunday roast this gently-sweet style was tuned for.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Lumpiang sariwa with the sweet garlic sauce — feinherb riesling and that sauce are secret twins.

anecdotes.text: 'Senior' honours Peter Lauer the elder — the cuvée preserves the grandfather's preferred gently off-dry house style, kept in the range under his name like a standing toast.

With this bottle the collection has climbed all three rungs of Lauer's pyramid: Ortswein (this Senior), Erste Lage (№ 21, still racked), Grosse Lage (№ 12, still racked). One grower, one grape, the whole German classification.
The single diagonal stroke across every Lauer label is the house trademark — drawn once, printed forever, and findable across a crowded shelf from three metres.

wines.name: Magnatum Vieilles Vignes Coteaux Bourguignons Blanc

window.note: Junior-appellation old-vine white: typically best inside six years. Drunk at eight — the far edge, deep in mature-Chardonnay territory.

rating.basis: estimated, calibrated to Vivino community data

wines.notes: Old-vine Chardonnay from a Vosne-Romanée family, bottled under Burgundy's junior label — Vivino's crowd files it under 'buttery and complex', which fits the style: baked apple, hazelnut and beeswax over a creamy middle. At eight years it was fully mature white Burgundy — honeyed, nutty, past fruit and into character.
wines.pairing_classic: Gougères warm from the oven — Burgundy's cheese-puff aperitif — or anything with truffle; the name is the serving suggestion.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Kare-kare. Mature Chardonnay's toasted-nut width meets the peanut sauce weight for weight, and the bagoong brings the salt the wine is quietly asking for.

anecdotes.text: Magnatum is Tuber magnatum — the white Alba truffle — and Bernard Rion is Burgundy's most famous truffle hunter, with trained dogs and hunts run from the Vosne-Romanée cellars. A white wine named for the white truffle: the pairing is printed on the label.

Coteaux Bourguignons is Burgundy's catch-all class of 2011 — it replaced the wonderfully honest name 'Bourgogne Grand Ordinaire'. When a Vosne domaine bottles old-vine Chardonnay under it, you're drinking the family's actual Tuesday wine at a fraction of the postcode's usual arithmetic.

Vosne-Romanée is Pinot Noir holy land — the village appellation doesn't even allow white. So the family's Chardonnay ends up in the junior bottling no matter how old the vines get, which is exactly why it overdelivers.

wines.name: Gevrey-Chambertin

window.note: Village Gevrey from an early-charming vintage; drunk at eight years, square in the generous middle.

rating.basis: estimated — consistent with community data; no critic coverage found

wines.notes: Village Gevrey in its open years: dark cherry with a licorice touch, an iron-filing mineral streak and that Gevrey sinew — the burliest of the Côte de Nuits villages, caught right in its generous middle.
wines.pairing_classic: Beef bourguignon — the village's own casserole.
wines.pairing_offbeat: Adobo flakes — duck if you can get them — over garlic rice. Gevrey's iron note and the crisped soy-vinegar bits are an unlikely handshake that holds.

anecdotes.text: In 1847 the village of Gevrey annexed the name of its most famous vineyard, Chambertin, and every Côte d'Or village copied the move — Puligny took Montrachet, Vosne took Romanée. Half of Burgundy's place names are 19th-century marketing.

Chambertin was Napoleon's wine — he had it follow him on campaign and drank it cut with water, which Burgundians consider the greatest crime of his career. Legend half-blames the retreat from Moscow on the supply running out.
2017 was Burgundy's exhale: the first full, frost-spared harvest after devastated 2016, and it made charming, early-drinking reds. Opening it at eight years was textbook.
